from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Traditional dimensions include points, lines, and planes.",
            "Some shapes defy these simple integer measurements.",
            "How complex is a shape filling more space?"
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Intuitive Limitation of Euclidean Dimensions", lecture_lines)
        
        # Mobjects
        dot = Dot(color=WHITE)
        line = Line(LEFT, RIGHT, color=WHITE)
        square = Square(color=WHITE)
        cube = Cube(color=WHITE, fill_opacity=0.5)
        
        lightning = VGroup(*[
            Line(np.array([i, -np.sin(i*2)*0.5, 0]), np.array([i+0.5, -np.sin((i+0.5)*2)*0.5 + 0.2, 0]), color="#FFCC00")
            for i in np.arange(-2, 2, 0.5)
        ])

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.place_at_grid(dot, "B2")
        self.play(FadeIn(dot))
        self.place_at_grid(line, "B4")
        self.play(Create(line))
        self.place_at_grid(square, "D2")
        self.play(Create(square))
        self.place_at_grid(cube, "D4")
        self.play(Create(cube))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FFCC00"))
        # Fade out Euclidean shapes, keep lightning bolt
        self.play(FadeOut(dot), FadeOut(line), FadeOut(square), FadeOut(cube))
        self.place_in_area(lightning, "B2", "E5")
        self.play(Create(lightning))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00FFFF"))
        label = Text("Complexity?", font_size=36, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(label, "A3")
        self.play(Write(label))
        # Flash the lightning bolt
        self.play(Flash(lightning, color="#FFCC00", flash_radius=1.5))
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Scaling a line by one-third creates three copies.",
            "Scaling a square by one-third creates nine copies.",
            "Dimensions relate number of copies to scaling factor."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Concept of Self-Similarity and Scaling", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#00FFFF")
        line = Line(start=LEFT, end=RIGHT)
        self.place_in_area(line, "A2", "A5")
        self.play(Create(line))
        
        # Visual of division
        segments = VGroup(*[Line(UP*0.1, DOWN*0.1) for _ in range(2)])
        segments.arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.5)
        self.place_at_grid(segments, "B3")
        self.play(Create(segments))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF00FF")
        square = Square(side_length=2.0, color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_in_area(square, "C2", "E4")
        self.play(Create(square))
        
        # Grid division 3x3
        grid_lines = VGroup()
        for i in range(1, 3):
            v_line = Line(square.get_top(), square.get_bottom()).shift(RIGHT * (i * 2/3 - 1))
            h_line = Line(square.get_left(), square.get_right()).shift(UP * (i * 2/3 - 1))
            grid_lines.add(v_line, h_line)
        grid_lines.set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.play(Create(grid_lines))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        formula = MathTex("N = (1/s)^D", font_size=36)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "F3")
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.wait(2)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Fractal dimension measures geometric roughness and complexity.",
            "Lightning bolts possess fractional dimensions between one and two.",
            "This tool quantifies shapes beyond Euclidean limitations."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Summary and Conclusion", lecture_lines)

        # Assets/Objects
        # Simple line changing to rough curve (placeholder representation)
        curve = VMobject(color=WHITE)
        curve.set_points_smoothly([np.array([0, 0, 0]), np.array([1, 0, 0]), np.array([2, 0, 0])])
        self.place_in_area(curve, "B2", "D5")
        
        # Slider value
        val = ValueTracker(1.0)
        
        def get_curve():
            d = val.get_value()
            points = []
            for i in range(11):
                x = -1 + i * 0.2
                y = np.sin(x * 5 * d) * 0.5 * (d - 1)
                points.append(np.array([x, y, 0]))
            new_curve = VMobject(color=WHITE).set_points_smoothly(points)
            self.place_in_area(new_curve, "B2", "D5")
            return new_curve

        # Use persistent mobject
        display_curve = always_redraw(lambda: get_curve())
        self.add(display_curve)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.play(val.animate.set_value(1.5), run_time=2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        # Represent lightning - just a jagged line overlay
        lightning = Line(start=self.grid["A2"], end=self.grid["E5"], color=YELLOW)
        self.play(Create(lightning))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: Fractal Dimension: Measuring the Complexity of Shapes

sections.title: The Intuitive Limitation of Euclidean Dimensions
sections.content: Briefly review traditional dimensions: 0D (point), 1D (line), 2D (plane), 3D (space). Introduce the problem: How do we measure the 'complexity' of a jagged, self-similar shape that seems to fill more space than a line but less than a plane?
sections.example: Compare a smooth straight wire (1D) versus a lightning bolt that fills space in a complex, multi-scaled way.

sections.title: The Concept of Self-Similarity and Scaling
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite: Scaling laws. Explain that if you scale a line by 1/3, you get 3 copies. If you scale a square by 1/3, you get 9 copies. The relationship follows N = (1/s)^D, where N is the number of copies, s is the scale factor, and D is the dimension.
sections.example: Visual animation showing a square being divided into 3x3 grids (9 squares total) as we zoom into one segment.

sections.title: Defining Fractal Dimension (Hausdorff Dimension)
sections.content: Formalize the math: D = log(N) / log(1/s). Explain that for fractals, D is often a non-integer, representing the 'roughness' or 'space-filling' capacity of the object.
sections.example: The Koch Snowflake: Each segment is replaced by 4 segments, each 1/3 the length. Calculation: D = log(4) / log(3) ≈ 1.26.

sections.title: Visualizing Complexity in Nature and Technology
sections.content: Show how fractal dimension applies to real-world objects that aren't perfectly smooth. Explain how a higher fractal dimension implies higher density/complexity.
sections.example: A lung's bronchial tree: High fractal dimension allows for massive surface area for gas exchange within a compact 3D volume.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Summarize that fractal dimension is a mathematical tool to quantify 'roughness'. Wrap up by connecting the theory back to the 'lightning bolt' from the intro, revealing it as a fractional dimension between 1 and 2.
sections.example: Final infographic: A slider showing how an object changes from a simple line (D=1) to a complex fractal (D=1.5) as the 'jaggedness' increases.
